title: Apple is betting on the App Store to give its smart glasses an edge over Meta and Google
summary: Apple smart glasses reportedly won't support Android phones.
body: TL;DR Apple is reportedly making Siri AI and third-party iPhone app integrations the centerpiece of its upcoming smart glasses. Internal prototypes are slightly thinner than the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses and feature flush cameras and a magnetic charging connector. Apple is targeting a June 2027 unveiling and a release before the end of the year, with no plans to support Android phones. Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro was supposed to usher in a new era of personal computing. Instead, Meta found success selling a much simpler wearable that barely looks like a piece of technology. Now, just days after Google and Samsung unveiled their Intelligent Eyewear to rival Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, fresh details have emerged about how Apple plans to compete in the increasingly crowded smart glasses market. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Apple is betting on Siri AI and its extensive App Store ecosystem to make its first smart glasses stand out. The idea is to let you order a Starbucks coffee, book an Uber, make restaurant reservations through OpenTable, or even buy movie tickets without taking your iPhone out of your pocket.

title: November Pixel Drop status: Here’s where the rollout stands right now
summary: A week after Google announced it, the November Pixel Drop and its biggest features are still missing on plenty of phones.
body: TL;DR Google announced the November 2026 Pixel Drop on November 10, but a week later many Pixel owners still haven’t received the update. Even users who have installed it say marquee features such as Create My Widget haven’t shown up yet. Google says the rollout will continue over the next few weeks, so it could be a while before every eligible Pixel gets everything. Google’s November Pixel Drop was supposed to be one of the biggest Pixel updates of the year. It arrived alongside Android 17 QPR2 a full month ahead of the usual December quarterly release, and it was packed with new features like the Create My Widget tool . A week on, though, a lot of Pixel owners are still staring at an October security patch, and many of those who did get the update are wondering where the new features went. The frustration started before the update even landed. Google usually pushes its monthly Pixel update on the first Tuesday of the month, but November 3 came and went with no update, even though the November Android Security Bulletin had gone live on November 2.

title: Bluetooth HDT could finally fix wireless audio quality, but there’s still one big problem
summary: HDT will be one of the biggest changes to Bluetooth audio in years.
body: News that Bluetooth has officially adopted its new High Data Throughput (HDT) specification should be music to audiophile ears far and wide. And there’s a good chance your future pair of wireless headphones could sound considerably better as a result. If you missed the announcement, Bluetooth HDT extends the capabilities of Bluetooth Low Energy (LE), boosting its maximum physical-layer data rate (PHY, pronounced “fie”) from 2Mbps to a comparatively colossal 7.5Mbps. That’s almost four times the maximum rate of conventional Bluetooth LE, and 2.5 times faster than Bluetooth Enhanced Data Rate (EDR), which tops out at 3Mbps. On paper, that’s a significant boost to data throughput, even accounting for transmission overheads. The Bluetooth SIG lists several potential applications for this extra bandwidth, including extended reality (XR), spatial computing, and AI-enabled devices. But what really caught my eye is the promise of standardized high-resolution and lossless audio . The only downside is that HDT requires all new radio hardware (we’ll get to the why later), which means all new smartphones and accessories are required before we can make use of it. You might have everything organized in a spreadsheet, but no one wants to scroll through dozens of rows just to see what’s happening next.
